A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PIVOT study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renumbering and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFT-versus-DPO experiments, model and data scaling, ImageNet and segmentation probing, gradient visualizations, and PIVOT evaluations and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds RL algorithm comparisons, sensitivity tests, filtered-data controls, and evaluations on additional visual and text-only benchmarks.

M1.justification: The PIVOT recipe, SFT/DPO objectives, encoder transfer procedure, and projector-reuse configuration remain unchanged. GRPO, PPO, and MPO are added experimental comparisons; they do not replace or introduce a new component into the default PIVOT procedure.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained VQA and visual-probing coverage, v2 adds HallusionBench and POPE; MS COCO and DetailCaps-4870 captioning; NaturalBench, MME-RealWorld, and VL-RewardBench; and text-only MMLU, HellaSwag, and GSM8K evaluations. Sections B.5–B.6 substantially broaden the evaluated task requirements and domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated GRPO-versus-SFT, PPO-versus-SFT, and MPO-versus-DPO-versus-SFT comparisons (Table 1 and Tables C–D). Tables K and P additionally compare PIVOT-based models with BLIP-2, SPHINX, SPHINX-Tiny, LLaVA-Next variants, and LLaVA-OneVision; these were not evaluated comparators in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GRPO/PPO training protocols, a learning-rate sweep, response-filtered 20K-sample controls, and post-training data scales up to 150K. It also revises the existing SFT learning rate from 1e-5 to 5e-6 (v1 F.1; v2 E.1) and changes the distribution-shift filter threshold from 100 tokens to 100 words. These reported setting revisions do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test learning-rate sensitivity (Figure A), whether preference-data formatting favors DPO using NoThink/Under30 controls (Table E), behavior beyond the original 40K data limit (Table L), and robustness on additional benchmarks (Table F). The earlier projector-reuse, downstream-data-scale, and full-parameter-training ablations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report six random seeds for segmentation probing and three-seed averages for representation alignment. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-run counts, or uncertainty-reporting practice for its added comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including GRPO versus SFT average scores of 65.9 versus 62.8 (Table 1), and a 150K-sample result where SFT exceeds DPO, 55.7 versus 54.7 (Table L). Main PIVOT aggregate scores remain unchanged. The retained full-training ablation also corrects misplaced category values in the 0.5B PIVOT row, from v1 Table D to v2 Table J.

T1.justification: Equation (1), the SFT/DPO objectives, and their mathematical definitions are retained. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's additional algorithm descriptions and mechanism discussions introduce no substantive formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims that RL improves visual representations relative to SFT and that PIVOT efficiently improves existing encoders, including against larger counterparts. The additional algorithm comparisons support the existing broad RL claim without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning unequal supervision per update and preference-data bias (D.4 and Section 7), and identifies reward-model confounding in the PPO comparison. It also introduces explanations based on response length and training-data overlap for the filtered-data and text-only results, plus qualifications about hyperparameter retuning at larger data scales.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a direct PIVOT code link and implementation details for the added experiments, including GRPO training steps and image resolutions, PPO checkpoint provenance, and response-filtering rules. Most existing hardware, data-access, and probing details remain intact. Conversely, Table 2 omits several encoder patch-size and resolution details previously present in v1 Table 1.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new benchmarks and RL implementations, cites BRAVE and SPHINX, and surveys GRPO/PPO implementations in Table B. Section D.3 elaborates the comparison with MPO and RLAIF-V, while retaining the established positioning around controlled post-training comparisons and underexplored vision-encoder effects.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the narrative sequence remain intact, with localized copyediting. v2 inserts a section on generalization beyond DPO, separates the existing PIVOT contribution discussion into Section 6.3, and regroups appendix explanations, discussions, and experimental details. These changes do not amount to an extensive rewrite of the retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous comparison and diagnostic tables and a learning-rate plot. Figure 11 is expanded to include downstream evaluation, incorporating material previously illustrated in appendix Figure D. The main PIVOT table gains a separate size column, and benchmark-table headers are revised; Table R unfortunately changes metric labels without correspondingly rearranging the retained values.

improvement.justification: v1's broad RL conclusions rested on DPO experiments. v2 substantially strengthens their basis through other RL algorithms, learning-rate sensitivity, SFT-friendly controls, broader evaluations, and explicit supervision/data-bias limitations. These address important generality and experimental-control weaknesses. The gains outweigh new reporting problems, including Table R's mismatched metric labels and claims of persistent DPO superiority contradicted by exceptions in Tables F and L.
